concepts.name: Savings Account
concepts.explanation: A bank account where you deposit money to earn interest over time, while still having access to your funds.
examples: Setting aside $100 each month in a savings account for emergencies
Keeping vacation funds in a high-yield savings account
tips: Compare interest rates across different banks to maximize returns
Look for accounts with no or low minimum balance requirements
Online banks often offer higher interest rates than traditional brick-and-mortar banks
furtherReading: Your Money or Your Life by Vicki Robin
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's guide to savings accounts

concepts.name: Checking Account
concepts.explanation: A bank account used for everyday transactions that gives you easy access to your money through debit cards, checks, and digital payments.
examples: Using your checking account to pay monthly bills
Setting up direct deposit for your paycheck
tips: Look for accounts with no monthly maintenance fees
Maintain a minimum balance to avoid fees
Monitor your transactions regularly to prevent overdrafts
furtherReading: Bankrate's guide to checking accounts
NerdWallet's 'How to Choose a Checking Account'

concepts.name: Interest
concepts.explanation: Money paid to you for letting a bank or financial institution use your funds, or money you pay for borrowing funds. Usually expressed as an annual percentage rate (APR).
examples: Earning 2% annual interest on a savings account
Paying 15% interest on a credit card balance
tips: Compound interest (interest on interest) significantly grows savings over time
Higher interest rates on debt mean paying more over time
Always pay high-interest debt first when trying to get out of debt
furtherReading: The Compound Effect by Darren Hardy
Khan Academy's lessons on compound interest

concepts.name: Credit Score
concepts.explanation: A numerical representation (typically 300-850) of your creditworthiness based on your credit history, used by lenders to determine loan eligibility and interest rates.
examples: Having a credit score of 750 may qualify you for the best loan terms
Late payments can lower your credit score by 50-100 points
tips: Pay all bills on time
Keep credit card balances low relative to your credit limits
Don't apply for too many new credit accounts in a short period
furtherReading: myFICO.com's 'What's in my FICO Scores?'
Annual Credit Report website for free credit reports

concepts.name: Credit Card
concepts.explanation: A payment card issued by a financial institution that lets you borrow funds to make purchases with the agreement that you'll repay the money, often with interest.
examples: Using a credit card for online shopping with fraud protection
Earning cash back or travel rewards on everyday purchases
tips: Pay your balance in full each month to avoid interest charges
Choose a card with rewards that match your spending habits
Understand the card's terms, especially the interest rate and fees
furtherReading: How to Get Out of Debt, Stay Out of Debt and Live Prosperously by Jerrold Mundis
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's credit card guides

concepts.name: Mortgage
concepts.explanation: A specific type of loan used to purchase real estate where the property serves as collateral.
examples: A 30-year fixed-rate mortgage to buy a home
A 15-year mortgage with higher monthly payments but less total interest
tips: A down payment of 20% or more helps avoid private mortgage insurance (PMI)
Consider your total housing costs, not just the mortgage payment
Shop different lenders to compare rates and closing costs
furtherReading: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 'Owning a Home' resources
Mortgages For Dummies by Eric Tyson and Ray Brown

concepts.name: Stock
concepts.explanation: A share of ownership in a company that may provide returns through price appreciation and dividends.
examples: Owning shares of Apple gives you partial ownership of the company
Receiving quarterly dividend payments from stock investments
tips: Invest for the long term to weather market volatility
Consider your risk tolerance when investing in individual stocks
Diversify your stock holdings across different companies and sectors
furtherReading: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing by John C. Bogle
Investopedia's guide to stock investing

concepts.name: Bond
concepts.explanation: A debt security where you lend money to an entity (government or corporation) that borrows the funds for a defined period at a fixed or variable interest rate.
examples: Purchasing a 10-year Treasury bond from the U.S. government
Investing in corporate bonds that pay higher interest than government bonds
tips: Bonds generally have lower risk and lower returns compared to stocks
Longer-term bonds typically offer higher interest rates but more sensitivity to interest rate changes
Consider your investment timeframe when choosing bond maturities
furtherReading: The Bond Book by Annette Thau
Fidelity's guide to bond investing

concepts.name: Mutual Fund
concepts.explanation: An investment vehicle that pools money from many investors to purchase a diversified portfolio of stocks, bonds, or other securities.
examples: Investing in an S&P 500 index fund that tracks the performance of 500 large U.S. companies
Using a balanced mutual fund that contains both stocks and bonds
tips: Pay attention to expense ratios, as lower fees mean more money stays invested
Index funds offer broad market exposure with low costs
Review a fund's performance history but remember past performance doesn't guarantee future results
furtherReading: The Bogleheads' Guide to Investing by Taylor Larimore
Morningstar's mutual fund research

concepts.name: Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF)
concepts.explanation: Similar to a mutual fund but trades like a stock on an exchange, typically tracking an index, sector, commodity, or asset.
examples: Using an ETF to invest in the entire U.S. stock market at once
Investing in a gold ETF instead of buying physical gold
tips: ETFs often have lower expense ratios than similar mutual funds
ETFs can be more tax-efficient than mutual funds
Consider trading costs if you plan to invest regularly in small amounts
furtherReading: A Random Walk Down Wall Street by Burton G. Malkiel
ETF.com's educational resources

concepts.name: 401(k) Plan
concepts.explanation: An employer-sponsored retirement savings plan that allows employees to contribute a portion of their wages to individual accounts, often with a company match.
examples: Contributing 10% of your salary to a 401(k) with a 5% employer match
Using automatic enrollment to start saving for retirement immediately
tips: At minimum, contribute enough to get the full employer match (it's free money)
Take advantage of Roth 401(k) options if available and suitable for your situation
Understand the vesting schedule for employer contributions
furtherReading: Retire Before Mom and Dad by Rob Berger
Department of Labor's guide to 401(k) plans

concepts.name: Dollar-Cost Averaging
concepts.explanation: An investment strategy of purchasing a fixed dollar amount of a particular investment regularly, regardless of the share price, to reduce the impact of volatility.
examples: Investing $500 monthly in an index fund regardless of market conditions
Using automatic contributions to a retirement account from every paycheck
tips: Helps avoid the pitfalls of market timing
Creates a disciplined approach to investing
Works best during volatile markets and over long time periods
furtherReading: The Intelligent Investor by Benjamin Graham
Vanguard's guide to dollar-cost averaging

concepts.name: Budget
concepts.explanation: A plan for how to spend and save your money, typically organized by income, expenses, and financial goals.
examples: Creating a monthly budget that allocates money for needs, wants, and savings
Using the 50/30/20 budget (50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings)
tips: Track your spending to understand where your money goes
Use budgeting apps to automate the process
Review and adjust your budget regularly
furtherReading: You Need a Budget by Jesse Mecham
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's budgeting worksheets

concepts.name: Emergency Fund
concepts.explanation: Money set aside for unexpected expenses or financial hardships like medical bills, car repairs, or job loss.
examples: Saving 3-6 months of living expenses in a high-yield savings account
Using an emergency fund instead of credit cards for unexpected car repairs
tips: Start small with a goal of $1,000, then build to 3-6 months of expenses
Keep your emergency fund in an easily accessible account
Replenish the fund after using it
furtherReading: The Financial Diet by Chelsea Fagan
Bankrate's emergency fund calculator

concepts.name: Inflation
concepts.explanation: The general increase in prices and fall in the purchasing power of money over time, typically measured as an annual percentage.
examples: If inflation is 3%, a $100 item will cost $103 next year
Needing to increase your retirement savings to account for future inflation
tips: Invest your money to outpace inflation (historically, stocks have beaten inflation)
Consider inflation when setting savings goals for long-term objectives
Look for investments specifically designed to hedge against inflation, like TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities)
furtherReading: Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index information
Inflation-Protected Investing guides

concepts.name: Diversification
concepts.explanation: A risk management strategy that mixes a variety of investments within a portfolio to reduce the exposure to any single asset or risk.
examples: Investing in stocks, bonds, real estate, and other asset classes
Holding investments across different countries, sectors, and company sizes
tips: Diversification can't eliminate all risk, but it can reduce it
Consider correlation between investments when diversifying
Revisit and rebalance your diversified portfolio regularly
furtherReading: The Intelligent Asset Allocator by William Bernstein
Vanguard's principles for investing success

concepts.name: FIRE (Financial Independence, Retire Early)
concepts.explanation: A lifestyle movement focused on extreme savings and investment to allow for early retirement and financial freedom, typically by saving 50-70% of income.
examples: Retiring at 40 by living frugally and investing aggressively during working years
Achieving 'Barista FIRE' where investments cover most expenses, but you work part-time for benefits or fulfillment
tips: Focus on both increasing income and decreasing expenses
Consider the psychological aspects of early retirement
Build flexibility into your plan to account for market fluctuations
furtherReading: Your Money or Your Life by Vicki Robin
Playing with FIRE by Scott Rieckens
Mr. Money Mustache blog

concepts.name: Opportunity Cost
concepts.explanation: The loss of potential gain from other alternatives when one alternative is chosen, a fundamental concept in economic decision-making.
examples: The opportunity cost of keeping money in a low-yield savings account is the higher return you might have earned in investments
The opportunity cost of buying a new car is what else you could have done with that money
tips: Consider opportunity costs when making major financial decisions
Balance short-term desires against long-term financial goals
Remember that time is often your most valuable resource with the highest opportunity cost
furtherReading: Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman
Khan Academy's lessons on opportunity cost

concepts.name: Social Security (United States)
concepts.explanation: A federal program providing retirement, disability, and survivor benefits funded primarily through payroll taxes.
examples: Receiving monthly retirement benefits starting at age 62 (reduced) or full retirement age (currently 66-67)
Disability benefits for those unable to work due to a medical condition
tips: Check your Social Security statement annually for accuracy
Consider delaying benefits until age 70 to maximize monthly payments
Understand how working while receiving benefits might affect your payments
furtherReading: Social Security Administration's retirement benefits guide
Social Security For Dummies by Jonathan Peterson

concepts.name: National Insurance (United Kingdom)
concepts.explanation: A system of taxes and contributions that fund various state benefits including the National Health Service, state pension, and unemployment benefits.
examples: Class 1 National Insurance contributions deducted from employee wages
Self-employed individuals paying Class 2 and Class 4 contributions
tips: Check your National Insurance record to ensure you'll qualify for full state pension
Understand the different classes of National Insurance and which apply to you
Consider voluntary contributions if you have gaps in your record
furtherReading: UK Government's guide to National Insurance
Money Advice Service's pension and retirement resources

concepts.name: Superannuation (Australia)
concepts.explanation: A compulsory retirement savings program where employers contribute a percentage of an employee's earnings to a fund that the employee can access in retirement.
examples: Employer contributing 10.5% of salary to your superannuation fund
Making additional voluntary contributions to boost retirement savings
tips: Consolidate multiple superannuation accounts to reduce fees
Consider your investment options within your superannuation fund
Understand the preservation age for accessing your superannuation
furtherReading: Australian Taxation Office's superannuation information
MoneySmart's superannuation and retirement planning guides
